articles.title: British Airways plane veers off Heathrow taxiway
articles.summary: The Boeing 787 Dreamliner bound for Lagos is delayed after its front wheel becomes stuck in grass.
articles.body:
A British Airways plane became stuck in the grass at Heathrow Airport after it veered off the taxiway.

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner bound for Lagos in Nigeria became stuck after its front wheel entered the grass as it was taxiing independently from the gate to the runway shortly after 10:00 GMT.

A spokesperson for the west London airport said they were continuing to assist the plane back to the aircraft parking area, adding that there were no injuries and no impact on wider operations.

A spokesperson for BA said: "We're very sorry to our customers for the disruption to their flight. Our teams are working to get them on their way as quickly as possible and are in touch with them to put things right."

It is not clear why the incident involving BA flight 75 happened. All the passengers disembarked safely and efforts to extract the aircraft are still taking place.

Richard Cooper, who was on the plane, said a lot of the passengers did not notice when the aircraft's front wheels overshot the taxiway and got stuck in the mud.

Cooper, 35, who lives in Aberdeen, was heading to Lagos on a business trip and only realised what had happened when the captain made an announcement.

He said: "The captain said something like 'the nose has ended up in the grass' and did sound a bit crestfallen.

"The crew apologised a lot for the discomfort and any distress, but it wasn't a traumatic event.

"If truth be told, I didn't notice it happening. We were on the taxiway doing about 5mph at the time. We were stuck there for some time but given regular updates from the flight crew."

Cooper said a plan to tow the plane back on to its route was considered but discounted quickly as its wheels continued to sink into the soft ground.

"Eventually they brought steps up to the aircraft on the taxiway and a convoy of buses to get everyone off in one go," he said.

Cooper said BA helped book passengers on to alternative flights, or into hotels if a same-day flight was not available. He was booked on to a flight to Lagos that departs later on Tuesday night.

He said: "I'm pretty circumspect about it. Speaking to people on the bus who were transporting back to Lagos from Canada, they were understandably more upset."

articles.title: How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
articles.summary: One of the key symbols of Russia's occupation of Ukraine has suffered major damage after a seven-stage attack by Kyiv.
articles.body:
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.

A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.

How did the seven-stage operation play out?

The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November , when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.

But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.

In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.

The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.

Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.

Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".

Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.

Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.

In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

articles.title: While working at an insurance company, John H. Johnson borrowed $500 against his mother’s furniture to start a publishing company in 1942; it went on to produce Ebony and Jet
articles.summary: Explore the inspiring journey of John H. Johnson, who transformed Black media with his groundbreaking magazines, Ebony and Jet, starting from just $500 borrowed against his mother's furniture.
articles.body: During the early 1900s, American society was deeply charged with racial tensions that segregated African Americans from the mainstream. Despite the abolition of slavery decades earlier, discriminatory laws and practices barred their access to public institutions and political participation. Against that backdrop, John H. Johnson saw an opportunity to create a publication for Black readers. While gathering newspaper clippings for an insurance executive, he noticed what those publications left out. His job involved reading Black newspapers and magazines and briefing the president of Supreme Life Insurance Company. The material gave Johnson a view of readerships whose lives were rarely covered by the press unless associated with crime.According to Entrepreneur, Johnson had arrived in Chicago with his mother in 1933. They spent two years relying on welfare during the Depression, the publication noted. He graduated with honours from DuSable High School in 1936, Entrepreneur added, and enrolled at the University of Chicago and continued to work at Supreme Life. He worked in the capacity of an editor for the company’s newsletter, the Supreme Liberty Guardian, and collected news about African Americans.When Johnson tried to obtain a bank loan for his proposed dream of starting a magazine, lenders refused his advance. He ended up putting his mother’s furniture up as collateral and borrowed $500. He used Supreme Life’s policyholder list and, per Entrepreneur, sent subscription offers to 20,000 households. Three thousand people paid $2 for an annual subscription and raised $6,000 for the venture, Entrepreneur reported.Three successful magazines and a revolution in Black mediaJohnson started Johnson Publishing Company in Chicago in 1942 and began publishing Negro Digest. The magazine’s first issue included contributions from poet Langston Hughes and civil rights leader Walter White, according to the Congressional Record for Jet’s 50th anniversary. Entrepreneur reported that circulation reached about 50,000 copies a month within a year after a series titled “If I Were a Negro”, which invited prominent white contributors to consider life as a Black person. The most prominent contributor was the former First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, who was among those who took part.According to the Chicago Architecture Center, Johnson introduced Ebony in 1945. The magazine covered Black achievement and community life. The magazine used photographs and reported on current affairs, civil rights legislation, freedom rides and marches. Ebony eventually reached an estimated 40% of Black Americans.Jet followed in 1951. It was designed as a smaller-format publication that readers could get through quickly. Its coverage ranged across topics of politics, music, arts and sport. The Congressional Record described Jet as a weekly publication with a circulation of almost one million. The magazine gave Johnson an avenue to transition into the advertising market. Entrepreneur said he persuaded companies that Black consumers were potential audiences, and advertisements that featured Black models attracted an effusive response. Mainstream sponsors at the time were reluctant to advertise in his publications. Johnson responded by setting up a beauty company and advertising those products in his magazines. Zenith Radio and Chrysler later became sponsors, as per the Congressional Record.Taking an empire beyond the page and into history booksJohnson Publishing Company eventually moved into 820 South Michigan Avenue, a building completed in 1972 and designed by architect John Warren Moutoussamy. The Chicago Architecture Center identified it as the first Black-owned building in downtown Chicago and the only high-rise there designed by an African American architect at the time.The building’s interior was designed with vivid colours, geometric patterns, textured surfaces, contemporary furniture and sculpture. As per the account of photographer and writer Lee Bey, the building personified “an Afrocentric modernism that was well-tuned, avant-garde”. Johnson Publishing Company occupied the address until 2010. The company’s interest extended beyond its two renowned magazines, Ebony and Jet. Entrepreneur recorded that Johnson added a book division, a book club, radio stations and Fashion Fair, a cosmetics business focused on Black women.Consequently, the building was sold to a property developer in 2017 and converted into rental apartments, as per the Chicago Architecture Center. Its original interiors were removed, but the Ebony Test Kitchen was saved from demolition by Landmarks Illinois and transferred to the Museum of Food and Drink in New York. Some original carpets, upholstery and wallpaper remained in shared areas. According to Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue, at around 6:25 a.m., crews arrived at the FLL after receiving reports of multiple injuries on JetBlue Flight 1717, which was arriving from Ponce, Puerto Rico, and had severe turbulence. articles.title: A California family sued after a therapist sexually abused their autistic daughter, claiming his employers ignored earlier warnings; the companies have agreed to a $3.8 million settlement as he remains in prison
articles.summary: A California family secured a $3.8 million settlement after their young, nonverbal autistic daughter was sexually abused by a behavioural therapist
articles.body: A California family secured a $3.8 million settlement after their young, nonverbal autistic daughter was sexually abused by a behavioural therapist entrusted with her care. The case renewed attention to the safeguards expected of organisations working with vulnerable children, particularly those who may struggle to communicate abuse. While the therapist remains behind bars, the settlement involving his former employer and its parent company raised questions about whether earlier warning signs were overlooked and whether adequate supervision was provided.Therapist abused child during home sessionsAccording to KRON 4 News, the abuse occurred in 2024 at the girl's residence in San Jose during behavioural therapy sessions. The victim, who is younger than 14, has autism and is nonverbal.The accused therapist, Alejandro Lopez Nunez, 50, of Santa Clara, was employed by Trumpet Behavioral Health. He also worked part-time as an instructional aide at Forest Hill Elementary School in the Campbell Union School District.San Jose Police arrested Nunez on June 9, 2024, after investigating allegations that he sexually assaulted the child multiple times starting in March 2024.Investigators became involved after a relative of the girl reportedly discovered the abuse and contacted the police. Authorities subsequently determined that the minor had been assaulted during therapy sessions at her home.Companies agree to $3.8 million settlementThe San Jose-based law firm Cerri, Boskovich & Allard announced that it secured the $3.8 million settlement on behalf of the family against Trumpet Behavioral Health LLC and its parent company, BlueSprig.Business Wire reported that the civil case focused on the organisations' responsibility to protect children receiving specialised care and therapy services.A central issue raised by the family's legal representatives was whether the therapist's employers had been informed of previous allegations involving inappropriate contact with children.According to attorney Mark Boskovich, a childcare provider reportedly warned Trumpet Behavioral Health about the therapist's alleged inappropriate conduct involving multiple children and prohibited him from returning to that organisation.The family's legal team argued that despite these earlier concerns, the therapist continued working for Trumpet and was subsequently assigned to provide services inside the home of a developmentally disabled child, with insufficient supervision.KRON 4 News reported that Trumpet Behavioral Health had previously confirmed taking action after learning about the incident, including terminating the employee, cooperating with law enforcement and initiating an internal review.Children's vulnerability is highlighted by communication barriersBeyond the financial settlement, the case highlighted the risks faced by intellectually and developmentally disabled children.Business Wire highlighted how nonverbal children may have limited ways to communicate abuse, making it difficult for families and caregivers to identify what has happened. Changes in behaviour, emotional distress or unusual reactions may be among the few indications that something is wrong.The figures cited in the firm's announcement underline the scale of the problem. Bureau of Justice Statistics data indicates that people with disabilities are more than 2.5 times as likely to experience violent crime as people without disabilities. An NPR analysis of Department of Justice figures also found that individuals with intellectual disabilities experience sexual assault at seven times the rate of those without disabilities.Broader questions about institutional accountabilityThe settlement renewed scrutiny of employee screening, background checks and supervision practices within organisations providing services to vulnerable individuals.According to Business Wire, Cerri, Boskovich & Allard has represented survivors with developmental disabilities in several institutional abuse and neglect cases. Its previous results include a $7.6 million settlement involving sexual assault at Mission College and a $6 million jury verdict against Sonoma County care provider Becoming Independent.For the California family, the $3.8 million agreement represents a significant development in their civil case.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Yemeni parliament approves law designating Houthis as ‘terrorists’
articles.summary: The law targets the group’s financing and activities as Houthis make advances in southwestern Yemen.
articles.body:
Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a law designating the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising the group’s activities and financing, as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government.

The vote, held over two sessions by videolink on Monday, comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. Parliament said it had deferred the bill, first tabled at a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, to give peace efforts a chance.

It noted that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the Iranian-backed group of brushing aside “all options for peace”.

Yemen’s cabinet approved the draft law on October 11. The country’s National Defence Council had designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States also lists the group as a “terrorist” organisation, and Saudi Arabia treats it as one.

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the legislation was formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, on Tuesday to be signed into law.

It runs to 55 articles and designates the group – including all of its political, military and civilian formations – “a terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction”.

It also toughens penalties for offences including seizing state authority, besieging cities, attacking civilians, laying landmines and attacking international shipping. Certain offences would carry the death penalty.

The law also sets out procedures to identify, trace, freeze and confiscate assets linked to the group and its affiliated entities.

The vote comes amid months of renewed hostilities after several years of relative calm on Yemen’s front lines. In late June, the Houthis announced an escalation against government forces and Saudi Arabia, saying the move was aimed at lifting what the group describes as a “blockade”.

In early September, a Houthi ground offensive on the western coast gave the group control of parts of Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after government forces withdrew from the port city of Mocha and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area.

Government forces launched an operation called “Dawn of Yemen” in early October to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. It initially made limited gains in recapturing territory lost on the Red Sea coast, but on Sunday, pro-government forces withdrew from those areas, allowing the Houthis to advance further.

Heavy fighting continues in Marib, al-Jawf and Lahij governorates, and the Houthis are pressing to take the city of Taiz, which the government and rights groups say is under a tight siege. The Houthis have also stepped up attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition says it is striking facilities that fund the group’s war effort.

The Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014. United Nations-sponsored talks and regional mediation have failed to end the war since then.

Ismail al-Suhaili, a political science professor and senior researcher at the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies, said the law marks a shift towards a tougher government position after the failure of peace efforts. Moving the designation from an executive decision to parliamentary legislation gives it wider legal force, he said.

He said it could complicate future negotiations by shifting their focus from power-sharing towards restoring state institutions, disarmament and UN Security Council Resolution 2216.

Al-Suhaili warned that the law could put additional pressure on banks, traders and companies operating between government- and Houthi-controlled areas and deepen Yemen’s financial split. Donors and aid organisations could also become reluctant to work in Houthi-held areas, which could disrupt the delivery of essential supplies to civilians. The Houthis, he said, could respond with further military escalation or with countermeasures targeting government leaders.

Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera the law was “a late step” but provides a legal basis for holding those responsible for abuses to account and compensating victims.

While the law narrows the space for political negotiations in favour of military action, al-Hamidi said, it does not entirely rule out a future settlement.

articles.title: Iran slams CNN, NYT for 'Iraq War-style propaganda' over alleged attack plots
articles.summary: Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday accused major US media outlets of spreading “Iraq
articles.body: Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Tuesday accused major US media outlets of spreading “Iraq War-style propaganda” and promoting false allegations. Their harsh remarks come after reports that claimed Tehran was considering attacks on senior Trump administration officials in Washington and developing underground missile facilities beneath dams.Araghchi dismissed the reports as “rubbish”, while Ghalibaf accused CNN and The New York Times of participating in what he described as a campaign to create support for a wider conflict with Iran.“In the past 72 hours, pro-Israel media have 'reported' that Iran is supposedly plotting to use chemical weapons in DC while building missile bases under dams. RUBBISH,” Araghchi wrote on X.“Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it. Nobody is buying it,” he added.The remarks followed a CNN report, citing seven US officials, that American intelligence had detected Iranian planning to potentially target senior members of US president Donald Trump's administration in Washington using a radioactive dirty bomb or chemical weapons.Separately, The New York Times examined possible links between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities.Iran rejects reports of alleged Washington attack plotAccording to CNN, US intelligence had picked up information suggesting that Iran was exploring plans for an attack in Washington. Two sources cited in the report said the alleged planning included specific locations and potential targets.The intelligence prompted contingency planning in the US, with officials holding several meetings over the past week to discuss possible responses.However, US officials remained divided over whether Iran had the capability or intention to carry out such an attack. Sources familiar with the assessment told CNN that the planning could be an attempt by Tehran to keep its options open rather than evidence of an imminent operation.The White House said it was monitoring potential threats but sought to play down the immediate risk. Spokesperson Lauren Bis said that “at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland”.Iran's foreign ministry also rejected the allegations. Its mission to the United Nations in New York said Tehran considered the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances “wholly illegitimate” and “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.The statement did not explicitly address the intelligence report concerning a possible dirty bomb plot.Ghalibaf, sharing CNN's report on X, wrote: “Same false flags, same war mongering, new logos.”He accused CNN and The New York Times of taking over a campaign previously promoted by right-wing media and alleged that billionaire Larry Ellison was behind the shift, describing it as “media capture”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ex-Reform Wales leader Dan Thomas faces no further action by police
articles.summary: Gwent Police says Reform MS faces no further action for arrest that led to him standing down as leader.
articles.body:
A police investigation into Reform's former leader in Wales has been dropped, two months after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Thomas said he had been "vindicated" by Gwent Police's decision that he should face no further action.

The arrest had led the Member of Senedd (MS) for Casnewydd Islwyn to resign from his role leading the largest Senedd opposition group , triggering a leadership contest and the election of Helen Jenner as his replacement .

Nigel Farage said he was "very pleased that Dan Thomas has been cleared", adding he had "stood by him throughout this process".

Jenner will remain as the party's Welsh leader, the BBC understands.

Thomas said he had been subjected to "false allegations" and had been "fully cooperating with the police".

"When this began, I said I had done nothing wrong. Today, I have been vindicated."

He said Farage, Jenner and Senedd colleagues had been "incredibly supportive".

"To my family and the people of Blackwood, my hometown, thank you for standing by me. Those constituents who have stopped me in the street to wish me well have been a real source of strength."

She added she was "so pleased to see a close friend having his name cleared".

Dan Thomas was picked by Farage to be the party's Welsh leader before the 2026 Senedd election.

The news that he was quitting as leader following the arrest broke on the same day that Sarah Cooper-Lessad announced that she was quitting his party for Plaid Cymru.

At the time of the arrest Gwent Police said a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, Caerphilly, had been arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

A spokesperson for Gwent Police said: "We take all allegations of assault and controlling and coercive behaviour extremely seriously, [and] a thorough investigation took place.

"The 45-year-old man who was arrested has been released with no further action."

articles.title: William and Catherine celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
articles.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.
articles.body:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.

One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.

Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Earthshot Prize 2026 - full list of winners

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries

Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution

Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind

The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.

As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.

The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.

Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.

As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."

The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.

Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.

articles.title: Religious ruling revives memories in Israel of Rabin assassination
articles.summary: Hostility towards Palestinian participation in Israel’s government fuels fears of far-right political violence.
articles.body:
As negotiations to form Israel’s next government continue, tensions across Israel have risen to an unprecedented high, evoking memories of the period leading up to the 1995 assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin .

In a letter published last week, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, invoked a principle in Jewish religious law known as din rodef, issuing a religious ruling that could be used to justify the killing of politicians accused of facilitating a government backed by Arab-led parties. The same principle was invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of Rabin because he had signed the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians.

“The Torah obliges me,” Axelrod later told the Israeli news website Walla. “I knew it was not easy, but if the Torah obliges, then we go. We are Jews, we make sacrifices.”

Axelrod’s ruling has prompted widespread condemnation and demands for a criminal investigation. The Chabad Hasidic movement that Axelrod belongs to has also distanced itself from his remarks.

Twenty former senior Israeli security, military and public figures, including former heads of the country’s intelligence agencies, have called on the authorities to investigate Axelrod. Separately, left-wing member of parliament Ofer Cassif and his fellow lawmaker Michal Rozin have also demanded an investigation, warning of the growing risk of political violence taking hold across Israel.

The controversy comes after Israel’s parliamentary election in late October, in which parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel won 19 of the parliament’s 120 seats. Parties opposed to caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hold a majority in parliament, but several members of the opposition have refused to cooperate with the Arab parties.

For many in Israel, mention of din rodef , or the “law of the pursuer”, immediately evokes memories of the tensions and incitement that led up to Rabin’s killing on November 4, 1995.

Rabin’s widow, Leah, directly accused Netanyahu – who was then the leader of the opposition – of helping to foster that climate of hostility. She pointed to his presence at a rally a month before the assassination, at which protesters displayed an effigy of her husband dressed in a Nazi uniform.

Amir justified his assassination of Rabin by arguing that the prime minister’s pursuit of the Oslo Accords endangered Jewish lives, echoing the reasoning now employed by Rabbi Axelrod, who claims that an alliance with an Arab-led party would place Jewish lives at risk.

This conflation of politics and religion, while hardly unique to Israel, amounted to “political theology”, Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani explained.

“By political theology, I mean the way ideas about God, sacred authority and the chosen people shape political life,” he said of the rules governing who is entitled to rule, who is allowed to belong and whose life must be protected. “Sometimes these ideas are explicit, as in a rabbi invoking divine law against an elected politician. But they can also survive in apparently secular ideas about the nation, sovereignty and historical destiny.”

“Someone who accepts Arab participation in government can then be portrayed as betraying a sacred community, and violence against them can become, in the eyes of a believer, a religious duty,” he said of the rationale behind Axelrod’s ruling.

“The threat of political violence is really high,” Cassif told Al Jazeera. “We all remember what happened in 1995 and the atmosphere that preceded Rabin’s assassination. This time it’s worse. Then it was just a few extremists on the fringe; now it’s the mainstream. They’re being openly encouraged by a prime minister who, I think, is ready to consider or do anything to hold on to power.”

Cassif also pointed to far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s own role in the atmosphere of incitement before Rabin’s killing. In October 1995, the month before the assassination, Ben-Gvir was filmed brandishing the hood ornament torn from the prime minister’s car, telling journalists, “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him, too.”

Fears of far-right violence have grown as coalition negotiations have dragged on. Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party have repeatedly sought to vilify Arab-led parties, both in their campaign ahead of the October 27 election and in their statements since.

Netanyahu has accused the parties of allying with foreign and hostile powers. And he used the swearing-in of the new parliament on November 10, anticipated to be largely ceremonial, to brand the incoming Palestinian politicians “terror supporters, haters of Israel” and denounce opposition politicians considering working with them.

Days earlier, right-wing protesters gathered outside the Herzliya home of Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader now tasked with forming a government, accusing the former general and chief of staff of being a traitor. One protester accused Eisenkot of having murdered his own son, Gal, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023. Turning his attention to Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, the protester told her she would be joining her son.

“Obviously, this is a tense time,” said political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University, who has made a study of political violence.

“The ultra-rightists will try to stop the process of changing regimes,” he said, drawing parallels with the January 6, 2021, attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of President Donald Trump. “Thus, it is a dangerous situation.”

“What Netanyahu is doing now is what he’s been doing for years: taking the Arabs, [and] the democratic Jews who work with them, and presenting them to the Israeli public as an overwhelming threat,” Cassif said. “Using minorities and their supporters as a scapegoat has always been a cornerstone of nationalist right-wing policy, and so it is in present-day Israel.”

President Bill Clinton presides over White House ceremonies marking the signing of the Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestinians with Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, left, and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, right, in Washington in 1993. Rabin was assassinated by a far-right Israeli in 1995 [File: Ron Edmonds/AP Photo]

articles.title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
articles.summary: Sunrise on the Reaping, the franchise's sixth film, is both criticised and praised by film critics.
articles.body:
Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".

But the Wrap praised its "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."

Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review .

"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".

The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.

IndieWire said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".

The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.

"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."

However, the Hollywood Reporter was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".

Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."

And Time Out's four-star review said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

articles.title: Who to watch in race to run Spain after 29 November elections
articles.summary: Spain votes on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule.
articles.body:
Spanish voters face a snap election on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule under Pedro Sánchez.

The left had hoped to focus on Spain's housing crisis, but the government has been buffeted by corruption scandals, a migrant crisis, and most recently rail disasters that left 115 people dead. Here are the key figures to look out for in the race to run Spain's next government.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) tops most of the polls and as leader of the conservative opposition since 2022 he is favourite to become Spain's next prime minister.

His pitch to voters is his experience and reputation as a capable administrator, with 13 years as president of the north-west Galicia region from 2009.

"It's called management: and it's what I know how to do, it's what I want to do, and it's the change Spain needs," he has told voters.

Feijóo has held public office continuously since 1991, and although he guided the PP to win the biggest number of seats in parliament in 2023, they fell short of an outright parliamentary majority. Sánchez's Socialist PSOE stayed in power through deals with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist parties and pro-independence groups.

Feijóo says the best outcome for Spain would be a PP majority governing alone, with support in parliament from far-right party Vox. His party has worked in coalition with Vox in four Spanish regions, and he has not ruled out a national coalition under strict conditions and red lines.

Unlike Sánchez, the PP leader is not well known internationally and his lack of English may hold him back on the world stage. Feijóo admits to making little effort to learn English but believes the "enormous problems" faced by Spaniards are of greater importance: "I don't know English, but I know how to govern."

Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.

He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.

Sánchez called the snap election eight months early , seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.

The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.

He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.

José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.

In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".

Spain PM pins hopes on housing crisis to help win snap election

Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike

Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.

Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.

Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.

He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".

The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.

His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.

He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.

Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.

Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.

Former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Frente Amplio (Broad Front) - which has lost many of its supporters in recent weeks to the Socialists and is currently polling in fourth place.

Previously called Sumar, the coalition was in government with the Socialists under leader Yolanda Díaz, but she decided she would not run again. Colau came into politics as a housing activist and fair rents and housing is one of her coalition's big policies.

Other parties on the left are contesting the election separately, including the pro-Catalan independence Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC) under Gabriel Rufián who has reached a campaign deal with Podemos under Irene Montero .

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies

Catalan centre-right pro-independence party Junts per Catalunya played a pivotal role in supporting Pedro Sánchez's government, even though it had just seven seats in the 350-seat Congress, and it may be central to post-election negotiations too. It was Junts' decision to reject the government's housing proposals last month that pushed the Socialist leader into snap elections.

Its lead candidate is Míriam Nogueras, who has made clear that Catalan demands come first for her party. Junts president Carles Puigdemont, 63, is planning to return to Spain after the election. He has lived in self-imposed exile since 2017 after leading Catalonia's failed bid for independence.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso , 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.

Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.

Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.

Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.

Socialist Carlos Cuerpo , 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.

He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".

In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."

Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

Carlos Hernández Quero , 30, has been a Vox MP since 2023, and speaks for the party on housing and urban affairs, taking charge of one of the most important election issues.

He is not regarded as the party's second-in-command, a position more commonly associated with figures such as Montserrat Lluís or Ignacio Garriga , but he is media-savvy and known for his clear, combative defence of Vox's economic policies and proposals.

Further to the right is Alvise Pérez , 36, a Member of the European Parliament who leads Se Acabó la Fiesta (The party is over). His party won three seats in European elections in 2024 and attracts voters disappointed with Vox. His party adopts a hard line on immigration, corruption and the EU.

articles.body: A nine-bedroom, 14,500-square-foot estate in Water Mill, New York, where the singer spent several summers in the early 2010s, returned to the market in early February 2026 asking $20 million. Built in 2009 on three acres bound by farms on two sides, the house was completely renovated by its seller. It has two full kitchens, a 16-seat dining room, a game room, a pool, a tennis court, a three-car garage and all-new landscape lighting. The house stands at the end of a long cobblestone driveway, hidden behind another home on Blank Lane for utmost privacy.How previous owners’ rental brought Madonna to Water Mill and the party's neighbours rememberedAccording to Mansion Global, the house was rented out by its previous owners, and Madonna was among their better-known guests. Out East’s listing describes the home as previously lived in by the singer and actress. Daniel Neiditch, president of River 2 River Realty, told Mansion Global that neighbours remembered her as an interesting neighbour who hosted some parties there. Around the same time, she bought a home in Bridgehampton that was completed in 2015, Robb Report reported, and she has also owned homes in London, New York City and Lisbon.Fully gut-renovated kitchens, fireplaces and common areas, plus a sauna, hot tub and catering kitchenAs per reports, Neiditch said the house was fully gut renovated, with the kitchens, common areas and fireplaces all redone. One of the two full kitchens seats 10 people, and a separate catering kitchen completes the cooking spaces, while a hot tub and a sauna are also listed. Inside, the listing details a finished full basement, two fireplaces, hardwood and tile floors, and a great room, family room, library, study, office, media room, exercise room, bonus room and an in-law suite with private guest quarters. He said the ample grounds and beautiful sunsets make the property stand out, and the listing highlights forever farm field views.From a $6.65 million pandemic purchase to $15 million and then $20 million, the home’s price historyThe seller, a New York-based limited liability company, bought the property in 2020 for $6.65 million, down more than 25 per cent from the $8.995 million asking price at the time, according to the Suffolk County and multiple listing service records cited in the report. Neiditch said the deal went into contract early in the pandemic, when prices had crashed, and that by the time it closed in October the market had already rebounded. A year later the seller listed the property again, first at $15 million and then at $20 million. Over the next few years it was intermittently offered for sale and for rent, with asking rents between $200,000 and $500,000 a month. According to Out East’s listing page for 336 Blank Lane, the home is still listed for $20 million, with River 2 River Realty listed as the broker.Disclaimer: Every fact, figure and quotation in this article is taken from, and credited to, the sources named within it. articles.title: A Van Gogh painting expected to fetch $180 million at Sotheby’s in New York faces a last-minute challenge: heirs of its former Jewish owners say a 1936 sale was forced by Nazi persecution and want the auction stopped
articles.summary: Descendants of German publisher Samuel Fischer have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs from its November 18 auction in
articles.body: Descendants of German publisher Samuel Fischer have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs from its November 18 auction in New York, arguing that the painting changed hands under circumstances shaped by Nazi persecution. The dispute, reported by The New York Times and subsequently covered by the BBC and The Art Newspaper, has put one of the season’s most anticipated art sales under scrutiny. The painting, also known as Blossoming Chestnut Trees, was created in May 1890, shortly before Van Gogh’s death. It carries an estimated value of $180 million and is being offered as part of the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection. If it achieves that figure, it would comfortably exceed the artist’s existing auction record of approximately $117 million, set by Orchard with Cypresses at Christie’s in 2022.The challenge centres on the painting’s ownership history during the years when the Nazis were consolidating power in Germany. Samuel Fischer, a prominent publisher who founded S. Fischer Verlag, acquired the work in 1909. His publishing house was associated with celebrated literary figures including Thomas Mann, Hermann Hesse and Alfred Döblin. Following Fischer’s death in 1934, his son-in-law Gottfried Bermann Fischer took charge of the publishing business. However, the Nazi regime increasingly targeted the company because of its association with Jewish ownership and writers whose works were banned. Bermann Fischer eventually left Berlin for Vienna in an attempt to continue publishing.The family’s representatives argue that the financial and personal pressures created by Nazi persecution played a direct role in the eventual sale of the painting in 1936. Their case also points to the restrictions imposed on Jewish people attempting to leave Germany, including the Reich Flight Tax, which required emigrants to pay a levy on their assets. According to reporting by the BBC and The New York Times, the painting had been deposited with an art dealer in Amsterdam before it was sold to collectors in Paris in 1936. The family maintains that the circumstances surrounding the transaction need to be examined beyond the geographical location of the sale.The heirs’ lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, has asked Sotheby’s to establish whether the painting was sold at a fair market price and whether the family would have parted with it in the absence of Nazi persecution. The family has also indicated its willingness to pursue a settlement guided by the 1998 Washington Principles, an international framework encouraging the identification and fair resolution of claims involving art confiscated or lost during the Nazi era.Sotheby’s, however, has maintained that its provenance research has not established that the painting was sold under duress. The auction house has acknowledged the concerns raised by the descendants and said it is engaging with them in an effort to reach a mutually acceptable outcome.You use AI every day. articles.title: Inquiry under way after Marr solar farm plans refused
articles.summary: Planning permission was originally refused but developers are appealing the decision.
articles.body:
A public inquiry into the decision to refuse planning permission for a solar farm in Doncaster is under way, a council has said.

Plans for the proposed 77-hectare site in Marr were knocked back in November last year following more than 1,200 objections, which included concerns about damage to agricultural land and the impact on nearby Marr Grange Farm Shop and Tea Rooms.

Enviromena, the company behind the proposal, launched an appeal, which will be considered during a seven-day inquiry at The Point on South Parade in Doncaster.

The company previously said the solar farm would generate £6.5m in business rates for City of Doncaster Council over 40 years.

The refusal was made possible by a late change to the designation of the land by Doncaster Council's planning officials, who labelled it green belt rather than grey belt, the Local Democracy Reporting Service reports. .

Grey belt is a term introduced by the Labour government, for "poor quality and ugly areas" of protected green belt, which can be built on.

Enviromena previously said it had won appeals in "very similar circumstances" elsewhere in the country.

articles.title: Four motorcyclists crashed after thousands of gallons of human waste spilled across a Kentucky interstate in 2022; four years later, an appeals court has upheld their combined $11 million pain-and-suffering award
articles.summary: A Kentucky court upholds an $11 million award for four motorcyclists who crashed after encountering a hazardous human waste spill on Interstate 24 in 2022, highlighting issues of negligence and safety in waste transport.
articles.body: A motorcycle journey through Kentucky turned into a horrific accident when thousands of gallons of human waste spilled onto an interstate highway, causing four riders to lose control and crash. The four motorcyclists were travelling at highway speeds when they encountered the dark, slippery material, fell from their bikes and slid across the contaminated road. All four suffered physical injuries and emotional distress, leading to a negligence lawsuit against the waste management company responsible for transporting the material.In a November 13, 2026, decision in Freedom Waste Services, LLC v. McAlpin, available on Justia, the Kentucky Court of Appeals upheld a jury's combined $11 million award for pain and suffering. The company had challenged the verdict, arguing that the damages were excessive and that errors during the trial had affected the jury's decision. However, the appeals court found insufficient grounds to order a new trial and affirmed the Lyon Circuit Court's judgment.Waste spilled from truck onto Interstate 24The incident happened on May 31, 2022, when James H. Watts, a professional truck driver employed by Freedom Waste Services, collected a full container of human waste from the Oak Grove Sewer Plant. The container was being transported to the company's landfill in Mayfield, Kentucky. It was designed with a latching mechanism and additional safety features, including a pin and safety chains, to prevent its door from opening during transportation.Around 30 miles into the journey, Watts noticed that waste was leaking from the container onto both lanes of Interstate 24. He pulled over, contacted his manager and attempted to secure the door using a strap to stop further leakage. Meanwhile, five motorcyclists travelling westbound behind the truck encountered the spilled material. They were riding at speeds of approximately 60 to 70 miles per hour when the slippery substance became trapped in their tyre treads, causing them to lose traction and crash.The riders were thrown from their motorcycles onto the road and slid through the human waste. Although they were wearing approved helmets and protective equipment, all four plaintiffs sustained injuries.Motorcyclists described injuries and medical treatmentFive motorcyclists initially filed a negligence lawsuit against Freedom Waste and Watts in April 2023. One of them, Joseph Von Herring, settled his claim before trial. The four remaining plaintiffs were Joseph McAlpin, David Hendriks, Jerry White and Mark Mudryk. Their injuries included bruises, abrasions and broken bones. The road rash they suffered was particularly serious because their wounds had been exposed to the contaminated material.According to the court record, their treatment involved medications, antibiotics, vaccinations and injections. Several underwent wound debridement procedures to remove contaminated material from their injuries. Some also required surgery or physical therapy and continued experiencing pain. The accident also caused emotional distress. The riders described the trauma of the crash and witnessing one of their fellow motorcyclists lying motionless on the road.During the trial, Freedom Waste acknowledged its responsibility to secure the transported load and prevent material from spilling onto public roads. However, the company argued that it had taken reasonable precautions and that the accident was unforeseeable.Jury awarded $11 million for pain and sufferingThe case went before a jury in May 2025. On May 29, the jury found that both Watts and Freedom Waste had failed in their duties and that their failures substantially contributed to the motorcyclists' injuries. The jury awarded McAlpin $3.5 million in pain-and-suffering damages, while Hendriks, White and Mudryk each received $2.5 million. Together, the awards totalled $11 million.The company challenged the verdict, arguing that the amounts were excessive compared with the riders' medical expenses. It also questioned the admission of a photograph showing repairs made to the container's latching mechanism the day after the accident.However, the appeals court found that the photograph was properly used to challenge Watts's recollection of the container's condition before the spill. He had previously identified a component in the photograph as being present before the accident, although it had actually been added afterwards.Appeals court rejects company's request for new trialFreedom Waste also argued that comments made by the motorcyclists' lawyers and other evidence presented during the trial had unfairly influenced the jury. The appeals judges rejected these arguments, finding that the company had failed to raise timely objections to several of the issues it later challenged. They also concluded that the jury's pain-and-suffering awards were supported by the evidence and that the trial court had not clearly erred in refusing a new trial.On November 13, 2026, the Kentucky Court of Appeals unanimously affirmed the Lyon Circuit Court's judgment. The decision means the combined $11 million pain-and-suffering award remains upheld, alongside the separately awarded medical expenses. The appeals court did not order a new trial or reduce the damages.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Maine judge rules school board committee discriminated against church over lease argument
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled Friday that Maine school officials discriminated against The Pines Church of Bangor with bad motivations over religious-based questions.
articles.body: A federal judge in Maine ruled Friday that the Hermon School Committee discriminated against The Pines Church of Bangor after its pastor requested a yearlong lease to hold Sunday services at Hermon High School, finding that religious bias influenced the committee's decision. In 2022, the church's lead pastor, Matt Gioia, reached out to the Hermon School Department to discuss renting space in the high school for Sunday worship services, requesting a yearlong lease rather than a month-to-month rental arrangement. After Gioia presented his proposal to the school committee, committee member Christopher McLaughlin sent questions through then-Superintendent Micah Grant, seeking clarification about how the church approached "issues of diversity, equity and inclusion around their messaging around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities." The questions also addressed its views on same-sex marriage, abortion and transgender issues. WASHINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT THAT FORCED KIDS TO HIDE BIBLES IN SEALED ENVELOPES MUST APOLOGIZE, PAY $275K Then-Superintendent Micah Grant also forwarded McLaughlin's questions to Gioia. Although Gioia received an apology from Grant regarding these questions, Grant and school committee Chair Jesse Keith later sought legal guidance on whether allowing the church to use school facilities would constitute "an unlawful establishment of religion" and whether denying the request would violate the First Amendment. Chief U.S. District Judge Lance Walker of the District of Maine wrote in his decision that while he did not believe Grant exhibited bias against the church, noting that Grant repeatedly worked to help Gioia through the application process, he found that at least three school committee members — McLaughlin, Stephanie Oiler and Karen Shorey — were improperly influenced by the church's religious identity or beliefs. "It appears that he based his decision directly on the Plaintiffs’ religious beliefs and its associated political and culture ethics that flow from those beliefs, and the religious nature of the proposed use," Walker wrote. "McLaughlin would have approached a lease request differently had it been presented by an organization that shared his personal beliefs. "I conclude that this qualifies as a sufficient ‘bad motive’ for First Amendment purposes as it has been interpreted and applied by the Supreme Court," the judge wrote while discussing Oiler's conduct. SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS Walker determined that the Hermon School Department's treatment and denial of the church's yearlong lease application violated its First Amendment rights and Maine's public accommodations law. However, the judge denied the church's request for a court order to block future lease denials. He noted that while the committee members had violated the church's rights, the church's attorneys had not established that the school's written rental policy was itself unconstitutional or adequately addressed the legal requirements for an injunction, including irreparable harm. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Hermon School Superintendent Barbara Sargent said the department was reviewing the decision and would consider whether to adjust its procedures. "While this legal matter has concluded, the Hermon School department’s dedication to its students remains unchanged," she said. "The department is committed to ensuring that this resolution does not distract from our essential work. We remain focused on providing an exceptional educational experience, supporting our professional staff, and maintaining a school environment where student success is the highest priority." Fox News Digital reached out to The Pines Church and Advocates for Faith & Freedom, which represented the church, for comment but did not immediately receive a response. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT In a press release, Advocates for Faith & Freedom praised the ruling as a victory for religious freedom. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This ruling affirms a fundamental principle: When public schools open their facilities to community groups such as sports teams, scouts and recreation programs, they cannot exclude churches simply because of their faith," Advocates for Faith & Freedom President Bob Tyler said. "The court saw through pretextual concerns about staffing, capacity and logistics and correctly identified the real motive — hostility to the Church’s religious viewpoint. The Constitution demands neutrality, and today the court enforced it."

articles.title: Three Manila moments that give Trump momentum going into talks with China
articles.summary: Forget the midterms. Trump lands in Manila to court ASEAN with trade, energy and AI deals aimed at capping China's sway over the South China Sea.
articles.body: Forget the midterms. President Donald Trump is still commander in chief, and he’s back on the world stage brandishing American economic power, with a big foreign policy agenda brewing. First stop: Manila. ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, is a group of friends and partners who just so happen to form a ring around the highly strategic South China Sea. These Southeast Asian countries feel the heat from China and want reassurance that the U.S. is dedicated to a free and open Pacific. Dining with ASEAN in Manila allows Trump to check in with China’s southern neighbors like Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, who together border the Strait of Malacca, the world’s busiest shipping channel. Trump wants ASEAN nations on our side and linked with deals on trade, energy, critical minerals and AI to cap China’s influence. The host is the Philippines, whose navy is constantly harassed by Chinese ships that claim "indisputable sovereignty" over Scarborough Shoal. I’m talking water cannons and ships scraping paint, even though an international maritime tribunal ruled in favor of the Philippines over a decade ago. Fortunately, U.S. relations with the Philippines are on firm ground under President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS Here are three moments from Manila that will give Trump momentum going into the next round with China and Russia. 1. Trump’s team is still at the top of its game. The undeniable blue tsunami of the Nov. 3 elections did not wash out Trump’s Cabinet. In Manila, you saw Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also the White House national security adviser. "How hot is Marco?" Trump jested during his ASEAN dinner remarks. It’s a fact. Rubio has become the most powerful and effective voice on American national security in years. Trump also praised his economic warriors: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. That should shut down rumors of a Bessent-Lutnick spat. Even better, Trump’s team has slashed the U.S.-China trade deficit from $382 billion in 2022 to $202 billion in 2025, and is on track to go lower as 2026 closes out. 2. Thailand trade deal. The U.S. trade deficit with Thailand hit a shocking $71 billion in 2025, with Thailand buying only $19 billion in American goods while sending us $110 billion of its stuff. That’s globalization for you. You can see why Trump was eager to sign this deal, which has been in the works for months and should increase Thailand's purchases of U.S. farm products, aircraft and other goods. TRUMP LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO KIM JONG UN JOINING HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH XI, PUTIN 3. Military power and the Quad. Flying all the way to the Philippines was worth it just for the Quad group photo. This informal diplomatic friend group consists of the U.S., Australia, Japan and aloof India. China hates the Quad. In Beijing, they call it the Indo-Pacific NATO. Not quite, but the Quad partners Japan and Australia are of inestimable importance to the military face-off with China. Both are military powerhouses in their own right, and they regularly host U.S. military forces and exercises. New F-15EX Eagle fighters just arrived at the U.S. Air Force base on Okinawa, in Japan. There is no love lost between India and China; a Chinese fighter jet barged into India’s airspace on Nov. 13, and India hasn’t forgotten that border forces clashed in 2020. Now it’s on to the 21-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, or APEC, where hosts sometimes hand out matching shirts, making for amusing foreign policy visuals: U.S. President George W. Bush and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Chilean ponchos in 2004, President Barack Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping in burgundy in 2014, or Trump in a dark blue silk button-down in Vietnam in 2017. articles.title: ‘Why shouldn’t we punish you for criminal contempt of court,’ Calcutta HC asks Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee, gives him 15 days to explain himself
articles.summary: Calcutta High Court asks Trinamool MP Abhishek Banerjee why he shouldn’t face criminal contempt over Facebook post; gives 15 days; orders security review.
articles.body: Kolkata: Why should punishment not be imposed on Abhishek Banerjee for criminal contempt of court, Calcutta High Court asked the Trinamool MP on Tuesday over his Nov 7 Facebook post that alleged that a section of the judiciary was bending under political pressure. Banerjee’s statements “prima facie amount to interference with the administration of justice”, the court held and gave him 15 days to explain himself.Justice Krishna Rao observed, “He has committed criminal contempt of court. He is not just a MP, but also the petitioner,” referring to Banerjee’s plea challenging his security downgrade from Z-plus to X despite alleged repeated attacks on his life.However, while disposing of Banerjee’s original plea on security recategorisation, the HC directed the state to hold a review meeting within two weeks to reassess his security cover. “This court is of the view that the authority should review whether the security cover requires enhancement by taking into consideration the incidents Banerjee has reported to the authorities,” the order stated.The social media remark at the centre of the legal war had come to the fore during last Thursday’s hearing on Banerjee’s plea, when additional advocate general (AAG) Billwadal Bhattacharyya read out the MP’s Facebook post in court. This had prompted Justice Rao to remark, “Your client is very intelligent. Please ask him to provide a list of judges who belong to BJP and those who belong to Trinamool.”Appearing for Banerjee, senior advocate Shoaib Alam had explained the context behind the post. “This is the speech of an exasperated man running pillar to post for your lordship’s protection — for himself and his family — for no fault of his own, but simply because the party he is affiliated with lost the elections,” Alam submitted.Following attacks at his Kolkata residence on his birthday, Banerjee had claimed in his Nov 7 post that it was the “seventh attempt” on his life in six months. His plea against the security reduction was then pending before Justice Rao’s bench.During Thursday’s hearing, when the AAG submitted that the next security review for all MPs would be held at the end of Nov, Justice Rao questioned the delay, asking, “Why wait for six months?”Banerjee’s counsel argued that given the spate of violence following the change in political dispensation, the MP anticipates political assassination. Pointing to state actions such as the removal of police kiosks outside Banerjee’s residence, he alleged a “direct nexus between the change in govt and the mala fide manner in which state authorities have acted.”While Banerjee’s counsel stated that his security had been reduced to two personal security officers on May 12, the AAG countered that he was provided with three. Submitting letters from May 12 and minutes from a May 29 review meeting, the AAG clarified that Z-plus security is typically reserved for the chief minister, governor and individuals facing severe threats, whereas most MPs are allotted X-category cover.“Banerjee’s residence continues to remain under high-grade security. Most of the incident petitions are still pending.
