articles.title: A videographer sued a media company for republishing his video of Michael Jordan breaking up a fight; a US appeals court revived his copyright claim, ruling that the full clip could act as a substitute for the original
articles.summary: A US appeals court has revived part of a videographer’s copyright claim against a media company that republished his footage of Michael Jordan breaking up
articles.body: A US appeals court has revived part of a videographer’s copyright claim against a media company that republished his footage of Michael Jordan breaking up a fight. In Richardson v. Townsquare Media, Inc., decided on 23 April 2026, the Second Circuit ruled that the district court incorrectly determined, at the pleading stage, that Townsquare’s use of the 42-second Jordan Video was fair. Because Townsquare republished the entire video, the court said it potentially provided consumers with a substitute work. The court vacated the ruling on screenshots, but affirmed judgment on a separate Melle Mel video, citing YouTube’s licence, and remanded.Michael Jordan video copyright case faces appeal setbackRichardson sued Townsquare, claiming that its use of his content violated his copyrights. The district court, presided over by Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, granted Townsquare judgment on the pleadings. According to the appeals court, the district court concluded that Townsquare's use of the Jordan Video was fair, that its reproduction of screenshots was de minimis and therefore not actionable, and that its embedding of a second video was permissible under a licence in YouTube's Terms of Service.On appeal, the Second Circuit reviewed the decision afresh. It stated that it "draw[s] all reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favour" and must vacate the judgment "if there are issues of fact which if proved would [permit a verdict for the nonmoving party]". The court summarised its conclusion by saying that it disagreed "in part and agree[d] in part" with the district court. The second video was an interview Richardson had recorded with rapper Melle Mel, in which Melle Mel criticised rapper Eminem. Townsquare had embedded it in two articles. The first covered the comments themselves, and the second covered rapper 50 Cent's response defending Eminem.Second Circuit questions Townsquare's fair use of Jordan videoThe Second Circuit held that the district court "incorrectly determined, at the pleading stage, that Townsquare's use of the Jordan Video was fair". The opinion notes that fair use is usually addressed at summary judgment. It adds that, to warrant dismissal of a complaint, "the fair-use factors must point decisively in the defence's favour". The court found that the district court had erred in assessing the first, third and fourth statutory factors. On the first factor, which covers the purpose and character of the use, the court called transformativeness "a closer call" than the district court's analysis suggested. It also noted that Townsquare is a for-profit entity, and assessed the factor as "at best, neutral". On the second factor, the nature of the copyrighted work, the court agreed with the district court that it weighed in favour of fair use, though it described the factor as one of "limited import".The third and fourth factors were central to the decision. Townsquare conceded that it republished the entire video, and the court found its arguments that doing so was necessary "premature and underdeveloped at the pleading stage". The opinion states that Townsquare "could have, for example, republished the text of the post along with a portion of the video", taken a screenshot of the post, or reported on the controversy with a hyperlink. On the fourth factor, the market effect, the court wrote that "it is plausible that viewers may not need to pay Richardson to watch the Jordan Video a second time if they can see it in full on Townsquare's website". The court concluded that Townsquare's decision to republish the entire video "rendered its use of the video a plausible market substitute for the video itself". It added that discovery may yet show Townsquare's use was reasonably justified, but that this was "not apparent at this early point in the litigation".Court rules screenshots in Jordan video case may infringe copyrightOn the screenshots, the district court had applied the de minimis doctrine, reasoning that a single still frame made up a very small fraction of the original video. The Second Circuit disagreed, stating that the doctrine "has no application here, as Townsquare prominently displayed the screenshots as the backdrop to the headline in each article". The court said the doctrine applies where the copyrighted work plays a negligible or incidental role. In its words, "the copyrighted work is the very subject of the secondary work", and easy identification "was indeed Townsquare's intention". It also rejected Townsquare's argument that the observability analysis in earlier cases applies only to "visual works" and not "video works", calling that argument "meritless". The court declined to affirm on the alternative ground of fair use, noting that the district court had not ruled on that basis.The Melle Mel Video was treated differently. The court affirmed the district court on that claim, holding that it was foreclosed by YouTube's Terms of Service. The opinion states that the licence granted to other users to use content "only as enabled by a feature of the Service (such as video playback or embeds)" "unambiguously covers Townsquare's use". The court rejected Richardson's reliance on Section 12 of YouTube's API Terms, and said Townsquare's alleged failure to follow other YouTube policies did not affect the scope of the licence. In a footnote, the court noted that the licence "on its face does not appear to cover Townsquare's use of the screenshots", so its holding "applies only to Townsquare's embedding of the video". The court vacated the judgment as to the Jordan Video and the screenshots from both videos, affirmed it as to the Melle Mel Video, and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.You use AI every day. articles.title: His $1 million gift helped build a Connecticut basketball arena in 1990; 36 years later, three daughters are suing after UConn added a bank's name under a $32.5 million, 20-year naming agreement
articles.summary: The daughters of Harry A.
articles.body: The daughters of Harry A. Gampel have sued the University of Connecticut and the state over the university’s decision to add M&T Bank’s name to the Storrs campus basketball arena their father helped build. According to reporting by CT Insider, NBC Connecticut, and FOX61, the family says a 1989 agreement promised that the building would carry the name Harry A. Gampel Pavilion in perpetuity.The dispute began after UConn announced a 20 year, $32.5 million naming rights partnership with the Buffalo based bank. The arena, which opened in 1990 as Harry A. Gampel Pavilion, is now being branded as the M&T Bank Center at Gampel Pavilion, a change the family says reduces their father’s name to little more than a footnote.A gift made with conditionsHarry A. Gampel was a 1943 UConn graduate, civil engineer, and real estate developer who advocated for a new basketball facility on campus. In October 1989, he donated $1 million toward construction of the 10,244 seat arena, which opened the following year as Harry A. Gampel Pavilion.According to the lawsuit, the donation came with specific conditions. The agreement required that the building be known as Harry A. Gampel Pavilion in perpetuity, that its exterior signage identify his name, and that UConn tickets, publications, releases, and public statements use that name.The family says those commitments were central to the gift. Their lawsuit argues that the university’s later agreement with M&T Bank violated the original understanding and diminished the visibility of the donor’s legacy.What changed at GampelOn October 21, UConn announced an expanded partnership with M&T Bank and said the arena would be called the M&T Bank Center at Gampel Pavilion. The university described the arrangement as part of a broader renovation and improvement of the facility.The Gampel family’s complaint says the new exterior signage gives greater prominence to M&T Bank Center than to Gampel’s name. The daughters argue that this presentation violates the 1989 agreement and asks the court to require UConn to restore signage that prominently displays Harry A. Gampel Pavilion.The plaintiffs are Debra Gampel Fischman, Margo Gampel Absher, and Linda Gampel Abrahamson. They filed the lawsuit in Connecticut Superior Court on November 11, seeking a mandatory injunction rather than monetary damages.The family’s central claimThe lawsuit says UConn entered the M&T Bank arrangement without the family’s prior consent or approval. It also alleges that the family spent more than a month trying to resolve the issue with the university but could not reach an agreement.Attorney Richard Weinstein, representing the family, said as per the reports that the daughters did not want to sue the university or create a public dispute. He argued that UConn’s response to their concerns amounted to delay rather than a direct resolution.Weinstein said the family could accept a joint naming arrangement, provided the Gampel name remained prominent. His position, according to NBC Connecticut, was that the arena could be called Harry A. Gampel Pavilion at the M&T Bank Center, but that the original name should not be eliminated.UConn’s responseUConn says it continues to honour Gampel and his contribution to the university. The university says Harry A. Gampel Pavilion remains an iconic and beloved building on the Storrs campus and is undergoing a major renovation.The university says it is expanding recognition of the Gampel name through enhanced back lit exterior signage at multiple public entrances, new interior floor level signage, expanded online recognition, and a physical tribute to Gampel and the arena’s championship history. UConn says these investments are intended to extend the life of the facility while preserving his place in its history.UConn also says it communicated with representatives of members of the Gampel family before the announcement and has continued to invite them to meet in person. The university says those invitations have not yet been accepted.A clash over legacy and revenueThe case highlights a tension familiar to universities across the country: the need to fund facilities through corporate partnerships, and the obligation to honour donors whose names are attached to campus landmarks. At UConn, the arena has hosted generations of Husky basketball fans and is closely tied to the school’s championship history.For the Gampel family, the issue is not simply a change in wording. They see the new branding as a weakening of a promise made when their father gave $1 million to help create the arena.For UConn, the partnership represents a significant financial commitment from M&T Bank and an opportunity to modernise an aging facility. The university says its goal is to make the renovated arena one of the best college basketball facilities in the country.What happens nextUConn has until December 8 to respond to the lawsuit. Until then, the dispute will likely remain focused on the meaning of the 1989 agreement, the prominence of the signage, and whether the university’s expanded recognition of Gampel satisfies the original commitment.Students on campus have already expressed attachment to the old name. Some told NBC Connecticut that they would continue calling the building Gampel Pavilion rather than adopting the bank centred name.The outcome may determine more than the wording on an arena facade. It could establish how far a university can go in adding a corporate sponsor’s name to a facility that was named for a donor under a promise of permanence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tensions rise over draft climate deal at COP31
articles.summary: Publication of the IPCC’s seventh assessment report becomes a sticking point at UN climate talks
articles.body:
A contentious draft deal has laid bare divisions between delegates from states participating in this year’s United Nations climate COP31 talks in Turkiye.

The 18-page draft “cover decision” published by summit cohost Australia on Monday includes a broad range of demands, including calls for a phaseout of fossil fuels.

The draft, as written, could make the negotiations “untenable”, said Wopke Hoekstra, the European Union’s climate envoy, adding that “the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change”.

“It’s very easy to draw red lines at the start of the process,” said Joao Paulo Capobianco, Brazil’s environment minister, adding that deadlocks can be overcome through “an adjustment in the wording” in the draft.

Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is steering COP31 negotiations, acknowledged that the text included elements “that not all parties agree on”, and that there might be “at least one more draft” introduced before the end of the week.

The talks are scheduled to end on Friday, but climate negotiations usually run into overtime as agreements must be reached by consensus, meaning even a single country can block the entire process.

The draft text includes a call for wealthy nations to achieve net zero emissions by 2030, and wording on phasing out fossil fuels that oil-rich countries have long resisted.

Consensus on the issue of net zero emissions at COP31 “might be very, very difficult”, said Michael Joseph, the environment minister of the island state of Antigua and Barbuda, adding that he “would love to see a commitment that calls on the phasing out of fossil fuels”.

“Emerging countries want to impose as many obligations as possible on developed countries. It’s tactical,” an official from a European country who requested anonymity told the AFP news agency.

“These things are obviously unacceptable,” the official said, pointing to a bloc of countries whose members include Saudi Arabia and India.

Saudi Arabia is also at the centre of another battle over the timeline for the publication of crucial reports by the UN’s climate science panel, which dozens of European, African and Pacific states want published before a crucial verification of global carbon-cutting efforts at the next COP33 conference due in 2028.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) publishes a series of reports every five to seven years that provide the definitive scientific assessment of global warming and inform global policy responses to the crisis.

The IPCC suspended its last meeting after failing to break the impasse, and a new session was set for December to resolve the issue, with Ilana Seid, chair of the Alliance of Small Island States, describing delays in publishing the IPCC’s seventh assessment report as “unjustifiable”.

The dispute has become one of the main issues being debated at COP31, which ends Friday.

On Tuesday, the kingdom’s delegation at COP31 defended its position on the publication timeline for the IPCC report, saying “Saudi Arabia is not seeking to delay climate science”.

Saudi Arabia “advocates publication timelines that allow sufficient scientific review, transparency and meaningful participation”, the statement said, without explicitly mentioning when Riyadh would like to see the reports published.

articles.title: ‘Squad’ member announces ‘Majority Priorities’ including reparations, abolishing ICE after blue wave
articles.summary: Rep. Ayanna Pressley dared President Donald Trump to veto reparations, Medicare-for-all and the abolishment of ICE as Democrats' new House majority sets up messaging bills.
articles.body: Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., unveiled a progressive legislative agenda for the incoming Democratic House majority Sunday, daring President Donald Trump to veto bold left-wing proposals ranging from reparations and Medicare-for-all to abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "We need to show people what Democrats can do with our majority. Reparations. Abortion justice. Medicare for All. Abolishing ICE. Childcare. Paid leave. And more," Pressley wrote on X. "If Trump wants to veto any of this, then the people will know exactly where he stands. And we won’t stop fighting until we win." 'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES The post included a graphic titled, "Rep. Ayanna Pressley’s Majority Priorities," including the message: "TRUMP WANTS TO BE MR. VETO. LET'S PUT HIM TO THE TEST." Beyond the policies highlighted in her post, the 13-point platform calls for extending temporary protected status (TPS) for certain immigrants, lowering housing and everyday costs, ending what she termed "Trump’s Iran war," blocking weapons shipments, halting data centers and rooting out corruption. Pressley’s push comes nearly two weeks after Democrats won control of the House in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. While the party secured House and Senate majorities that will take office in January, Democrats remain well short of the two-thirds supermajority required in each chamber of Congress to override a presidential veto, setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing Trump to reject progressive legislation. At the top of Pressley’s list is H.R. 40, the Commission to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals for African Americans Act, which Pressley reintroduced in January 2025 to examine the legacy of slavery and develop reparations proposals. Other progressive lawmakers have pushed even further; in March 2026, Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., introduced separate legislation, H.R. 7927, to establish a federal commission to "study and distribute land reparations" to descendants of enslaved people. The Department of Justice is involved in a lawsuit against Evanston, Illinois, for launching a reparations initiative that provides $25,000 in cash or housing-related financial assistance to eligible Black residents and descendants of Black residents. In 2019, Evanston became the first U.S. city to approve a municipal reparations plan, pledging $10 million over a decade funded by a local cannabis tax. While progressive Democrats have long championed reparations, the issue has repeatedly drawn pushback from moderate members of the party who view it as a political liability. TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES A DOJ official told Fox News Digital that while the agency "does not comment on the legislative priorities of members of Congress or speculate about future legislation, any legislation that allocates public benefits based on race is unconstitutional and debating such bills would be a waste of Congress’s time." "Our lawsuit challenging Evanston's reparations program is about the Constitution and federal civil rights law," the spokesperson said. "As alleged in our filing, the program provides housing-related financial assistance based on race, which violates the equal protection clause and the Fair Housing Act. The department's position is set out in court filings. "The department enforces federal civil rights laws, which protect all Americans equally regardless of race. We will continue to do so." Pressley's renewed call to abolish ICE drew a sharp rebuke from the Trump administration. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Fox News Digital Pressley should be grateful the administration has removed "dangerous criminals from her district." "America’s brave ICE agents put their lives on the line every day to enforce U.S. law and arrest criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, rapists and murderers," the spokesperson said. "Representative [Pressley] should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district — NOT vilifying law enforcement. This type of rhetoric is contributing to a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line. "Since day one, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump’s promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens, including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members and terrorists," the spokesperson added. "Nearly 60% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. More than 3 million illegal aliens are out of the country and counting. Our message is clear: If you come to our country illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you and we will deport you." 'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS DHS also warned that anti-ICE rhetoric from elected officials has coincided with a surge in targeted violence against federal immigration officers. "Attacks and demonization of ICE law enforcement is wrong. Because of smears like this, our ICE officers are now facing a 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson said. articles.title: California sheriff's deputy, special officer put on leave after 5-second conversation with ICE agents
articles.summary: Two California sheriff's department employees are on administrative leave after video captured a five-second ICE exchange outside a county jail.
articles.body: Two California sheriff's department employees have been placed on administrative leave pending an investigation after a five-second conversation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers outside a county jail. The Orange County Sheriff's Department announced Friday that surveillance video captured the Oct. 31 exchange outside the Intake Release Center. A deputy and a sheriff’s special officer (SSO) were seen leaving the facility, approaching an SUV and "appearing to have a five-second conversation" with ICE officers, the department said. Moments after the sheriff's deputy and security officer walked away, a second vehicle arrived. EXCLUSIVE: LA ICE DIRECTOR REVEALS OFFICERS FOLLOWED HOME, HARASSED AS POLICE FAIL TO HELP IN SANCTUARY CITY The ICE officers exited both vehicles and entered a public courtyard outside the visitor's entrance. There, they detained a man who appeared to be hiding, according to the sheriff's department. Authorities did not release the man's name or why he was detained. NEW MAINE LAW LIMITS POLICE COOPERATION WITH FEDERAL IMMIGRATION OFFICIALS The sheriff's department has opened an internal investigation into the incident, which raises questions regarding compliance with California's Values Act (SB 54), a state law that strictly limits how local law enforcement can assist federal immigration authorities. Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes said his agency takes public safety and state compliance seriously. MARYLAND SHERIFF TORCHES DEMOCRATS OVER LAW HE SAYS PUTS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FIRST "I will fully cooperate with ICE to the extent the law allows to prevent serious criminal offenders from returning to the communities they have preyed upon," Barnes said in a statement. "Personnel acting outside the law and Department policy will be held appropriately accountable. "We will enforce state and local laws equally, without bias, and without concern for anyone’s citizenship," he added. "I want the community to continue to feel safe in calling for assistance, reporting crime and visiting the jail regardless of their immigration status." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security noted that seven of the 10 safest cities in the United States partner with ICE. "Because some sanctuary states including California refuse to work with ICE law enforcement, criminal illegal aliens are released from jails into American communities to perpetuate more crimes," the statement said. "Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country." "Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in California," the statement added. Local law enforcement worked with DHS, including helping to make 40,000 arrests in Florida and a two-week operation in West Virginia that resulted in the arrest of over 650 illegal aliens, the agency said.

articles.title: New Nvidia boss says momentum goes on as firm reports bumper results after Huang quits
articles.summary: Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang earlier on Tuesday offered to return, despite the board's disinterest.
articles.body:
Nvidia's interim chief executive Collette Kress said the company's rapid growth is on track as it topped $100bn in quarterly sales for the first time.

In the company's first results since the dramatic exit of founder Jensen Huang, Kress said Nvidia's "roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater".

The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company recovering some recent losses in after-hours trading.

Earlier on Tuesday Huang, said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following two alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a possible spy for China.

"The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones told investors on Tuesday.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.

Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter.

Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."

articles.title: US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline
articles.summary: The National Security Agency says a "temporary degradation" affected some internal systems but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected.
articles.body:
A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports.

The NSA - America's largest intelligence organisation - said it had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected.

The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information.

It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure.

"While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.

"NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

It did not specify when the issue began, nor when it would be resolved.

The issue was not a cyberattack, multiple US news outlets reported.

Tens of thousands of people work at the NSA, which is responsible for collecting signals intelligence, overseeing cyber threats, and protecting US government communications.

Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday.

Sources familiar with the situation told CBS that operations at the NSA's headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, had not been affected but that some activities had been redirected to other facilities around the country.

Tuesday's outage follows a series of technological outages.

Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights.

On Monday, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident.

articles.title: Israeli parliament elects new Knesset speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents
articles.summary: JERUSALEM — The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The newly-elected speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu. Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election. He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours. “The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favor of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote. The vote took place weeks after Oct. 27 parliamentary elections in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently given the task by Israel’s president to try to form a new coalition government. Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition. As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly-sworn in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda. They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and to reverse laws to limit the powers of the judiciary. The speaker helps set the agenda Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira with the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. “It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said. Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker. Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Currently a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, Roy Folkman, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed. If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would likely give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee. Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone,” Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed.” Time is limited to pass legislation Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee, and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out. Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritize rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances. “It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said. Establishing a body to investigate the Oct. 7 attack would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed. Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability. The scars of Oct. 7 were on display in the chamber on Tuesday. Hours into the debate, Talik Gvili, a Likud member whose son was a police officer killed by Palestinian militants on Oct. 7, interrupted Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Arab Joint List, as he was criticizing far-right Knesset members for racist comments. “Who killed my son?” Gvili shouted. “Why are you starting to pin it on me?” Tibi replied. “Don’t ask such a question to an Arab member of the Knesset.” A shouting match ensued, with Tibi from the dais urging Gvili not to rely on insinuation. “The one who committed the murder is Hamas. The one responsible is your prime minister,” he said.
